account:
Today there seems to be an effort to arrange grain and bread supplies through trade or credit, although I do not yet know the full arrangement. During my morning mill inspection I found eighty hay bales in the mill stall, posted at two emeralds each. The neighbour told me that builder and freight wanted nineteen bales and were offering thirty-two oak planks and agreed services; the innkeeper also urgently needed grain and had mentioned credit or trade. That suggests difficulty paying rather than an actual absence of grain. At 11:26 I personally saw builder give oak planks to baker, which may be part of that arrangement, but I have not confirmed the terms or seen grain change hands.

Several residents have repeated a vague report of a 'bridge or port change' at the bakery. One associated baker and innkeeper with it, and another version included freight. Nobody has explained what changed. It could concern transport or supply arrangements, but I cannot yet say that any bridge, ferry, or port operation has actually changed. Reports of innkeeper carrying sacks of bread at the bakery and plaza, and baker carrying bread at the inn, suggest bread deliveries or exchanges; these reports alone do not establish anything improper.

There is also unfinished town business: the treasury held 128 emeralds but no account records, and the secretary's earlier inquiry found no council records identifying who holds the missing account figures. I have no evidence connecting that problem to the grain negotiations. I am now back at the town hall for the thirteen o'clock council letters appointment, with the secretary waiting nearby. Later I have tea with the neighbour at three and the approved great-hall lighting inspection with builder at six.
